evidence.claim: Mountain passes and mining towns
evidence.quote: The mines petered out, and the town is now known for its beautiful, high alpine scenery, skiing, fishing, and switchback roads through old mining country. The route then runs through Bobcat Pass

evidence.claim: The Enchanted Circle loops from Taos through mountain passes and the Moreno Valley, encircling Wheeler Peak, New Mexico’s highest mountain.
evidence.quote: The byway encircles Wheeler Peak (13,161 feet (4,011 m)) of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains. It is the tallest mountain in New Mexico.

evidence.claim: loops from Taos through mountain passes and the Moreno Valley
evidence.quote: It begins and ends in Taos, New Mexico.

evidence.claim: The New Mexico Tourism Department emphasizes alpine scenery, fishing, skiing and switchback roads through old mining country.
evidence.quote: The mines petered out, and the town is now known for its beautiful, high alpine scenery, skiing, fishing, and switchback roads through old mining country.

evidence.claim: The U.S. Forest Service designated the circle a National Forest Scenic Byway in 1989; state scenic-byway designation followed in 1998.
evidence.quote:
The Enchanted Circle Scenic Byway was named a New Mexico Scenic Byways on July 31, 1998.
It was designated as a National Forest Scenic Byway by the U.S. Forest Service on December 14, 1989.

evidence.claim: The drive passes lakes and streams as well as historic towns, with ski resorts and recreation parks close to the route.
evidence.quote: The scenic byway passes through historic towns, alongside lakes and streams, and near ski resorts and recreational parks.

evidence.claim: Palo Flechado Pass carried travelers toward Taos before the numbered highways.
evidence.quote: It continued to be used by Native Americans, Spaniards, and Europeans on journeys to Taos.

evidence.claim: Comanche, Kiowa and Apache used the pass on a trail from the plains before the Spanish arrived.
evidence.quote: Comanche, Kiowa, and Apache used the mountain pass on a trail from the plains to and then alongside the Cimarron River (also called La Flecha) before the arrival of the Spanish.

evidence.claim: In the highway era, the road into Taos from the northeast was U.S. 485 in 1927; U.S. 64 replaced that number in 1931.
evidence.quote: In 1927 the road into Taos from the northeast was highway 485, a branch of 85 from Raton, New Mexico.

evidence.claim: U.S. 64 replaced that number in 1931
evidence.quote: In 1931, U.S. 485 was replaced by U.S. Route 64.

evidence.claim: The scenic circle later joined this approach to the roads through Questa and Red River.
evidence.quote:
NM 522 between Taos and Questa
NM 38 between Questa, Red River, and Eagle Nest

evidence.claim: From Taos, drive east on U.S. 64 through the Rio Fernando canyon and across Palo Flechado Pass toward the Moreno Valley.
evidence.quote: From Angel Fire, west on US 64 is the Palo Flechado Pass

evidence.claim: through the Rio Fernando canyon
evidence.quote: Campsites, canyon trails, picnic areas, and artist's studios are located in the Canyon of the Rio Fernando de Taos.

evidence.claim: The Vietnam Veterans Memorial is near Angel Fire at the valley’s southern end.
evidence.quote: At the southernmost point of the valley  is the Vietnam Veterans Memorial State Park.

evidence.claim: Continue north to Eagle Nest, then cross Bobcat Pass on NM 38 to Red River and Questa.
evidence.quote: NM 38 between Questa, Red River, and Eagle Nest

evidence.claim: Continue north to Eagle Nest
evidence.quote: At the eastern edge of the scenic byway is the Moreno Valley, which lies between Eagle Nest and Angel Fire.

evidence.claim: cross Bobcat Pass on NM 38
evidence.quote: It is located on NM 38 between Eagle Nest, New Mexico and Red River

evidence.claim: NM 522 leads south through Arroyo Hondo and back to Taos.
evidence.quote: Head nine miles north of Taos on NM 522 to Arroyo Hondo.

evidence.claim: The chapel near Angel Fire was dedicated on May 22, 1971, to honor veterans of the Vietnam War.
evidence.quote: The Chapel was dedicated May 22, 1971.

evidence.claim: In 1987, Congress recognized the Disabled American Veterans Vietnam Veterans National Memorial as a memorial of national significance.
evidence.quote: As the "Disabled American Veterans Vietnam Veterans National Memorial", it was recognized by the United States Congress as a "memorial of national significance" in 1987.

evidence.claim: The site lies near U.S. 64, at the southern end of the Moreno Valley.
evidence.quote: Vietnam Veterans Memorial is a national memorial established in honor of Vietnam War veterans, near United States Highway 64 in Angel Fire, New Mexico.

evidence.claim: at the southern end of the Moreno Valley
evidence.quote: At the southernmost point of the valley  is the Vietnam Veterans Memorial State Park.

evidence.claim: A railway project preceded the lake at Eagle Nest.
evidence.quote: Before this, the St. Louis, Rocky Mountain and Pacific Railway did some grading work in 1907 on an unfinished extension from its terminus at Ute Park to Taos, including boring a tunnel here.

evidence.claim: In 1907, the St. Louis, Rocky Mountain and Pacific Railway graded part of an extension from Ute Park toward Taos and bored a tunnel here, but the extension remained unfinished.
evidence.quote: Before this, the St. Louis, Rocky Mountain and Pacific Railway did some grading work in 1907 on an unfinished extension from its terminus at Ute Park to Taos, including boring a tunnel here.

evidence.claim: Eagle Nest Dam impounded the Cimarron River in 1918, creating the reservoir.
evidence.quote: The lake itself is a man-made reservoir created when the Cimarron River was impounded by the Eagle Nest Dam in 1918.

evidence.claim: The lake lies at 8,300 feet in a glacial valley on Wheeler Peak’s slopes.
evidence.quote: Eagle Nest Lake is at an elevation of 8,300 feet (2,500 m), making it an alpine lake, and it is situated in a glacial valley on the slopes of Wheeler Peak, New Mexico's highest mountain.

evidence.claim: The village occupies its northern end; originally called Therma, it took the name Eagle Nest in the 1930s.
evidence.quote: Originally named Therma, the village was renamed Eagle Nest in the 1930s.

evidence.claim: The village occupies its northern end
evidence.quote: The village is at the north end of Eagle Nest Lake, a reservoir on the Cimarron River.

evidence.claim: The reservoir became the main attraction of Eagle Nest Lake State Park, established in 2004.
evidence.quote: It was established on July 3, 2004. Its main attraction is a 2,400-acre (970 ha) lake

evidence.claim: Red River takes its name from the perennial stream that flows through town from Wheeler Peak’s northern slopes.
evidence.quote: It was named after the perennial stream, Red River, that flows through the town, coming from the northern slopes of Wheeler Peak.

evidence.claim: Before the mining town developed, Jicarilla Apache and Utes used the area as a summer hunting ground.
evidence.quote: Prior to the arrival of European-Americans, the area now occupied by Red River was used as a summer hunting ground by the Jicarilla Apache and Utes,

evidence.claim: Miners arrived from nearby Elizabethtown in the late nineteenth century, drawn by gold strikes.
evidence.quote: The town of Red River had its beginnings late in the 19th century, when miners from nearby Elizabethtown in the Moreno Valley were drawn in by gold strikes in the area

evidence.claim: Mining peaked in 1897 and declined by 1905, but trout fishing and summer visitors helped the town survive.
evidence.quote: Mining hit its peak in 1897, and by 1905 the mining and the population dwindled but the town survived, gaining a reputation as a great getaway from hot weather and as a trout fishing paradise.

evidence.claim: By the last serious mining efforts in 1931, tourism was already its principal livelihood.
evidence.quote: The last serious mining efforts extended until 1931. By that time tourism had become the principal economic livelihood.

evidence.claim: The resort town is surrounded by Carson National Forest.
evidence.quote: Red River is located in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains, part of the southern Rocky Mountains, and is surrounded by the Carson National Forest.
